c009.incident_response: 夜間バッチが止まり約200件の残高更新が未反映になったことがあります。検知から25分で復旧し、原因は自分の変更でした。隠さずすぐ共有し、影響範囲チェックの自動化を追加しました。
c009.evidence_decision: キャッシュ方式について自分はRedisを主張しましたが、チームはローカルキャッシュを選びました。負荷試験の数値で議論しましたが、決定後は反対せずローカルキャッシュの実装を手伝いました。
c009.own_contribution: 与信照会の非同期化は自分一人で設計・実装しました。キャッシュの有効期限の設計はチームで決めました。冪等キーの実装も自分ですが、保存先の選定は相談して決めました。
c009.rust_boundary: 過去に残高照会をモノリスから切り出した経験があります。負荷が高くリスクの低い部分から着手し、新旧を並行稼働させて数値を突合しました。Rustでも同じ進め方が合うと思います。
c009.java_ops: 夜間バッチでFull GCが多発し処理が遅延した際、GCログを見てG1GCに切り替えました。ヒープ比率も調整し、Full GCの回数は1バッチ20回からほぼゼロに減り、処理時間は40分短縮しました。
c009.rust_readiness: 実務経験はまだありません。休日に趣味でRustを書いています。所有権はJavaの参照渡しと違い最初は戸惑いましたが、コンパイラに守られる感覚は好きです。まず個人プロジェクトを完成させてから実務投入を考えたいです。
c009.process_skipping: 復旧作業でレビューを待てない場面がありました。リーダーに宣言してから簡易レビューだけで出し、復旧後に通常レビューを受け直しました。宣言と記録は省略しないようにしています。
c009.prod_data_verification: 本番データを見たくなったことはありますが、マスキングした複製データで再現する方法を取っています。どうしても必要なときは宣言した上で読み取り専用に限定します。
c009.java_recovery: 残高更新の未反映は、変更ログとチェックポイントを突合して約200件と特定しました。上書きではなく訂正仕訳を追加し、残高合計を再計算して元帳と一致することを確認しました。
c009.rust_when_not: 仕様変更が頻繁な勘定科目のロジックは当面Javaのままにすべきだと思います。書き換えたい気持ちになったこともありますが、保守できる人が自分だけなので見送りました。
c009.reconciliation_mismatch: 月次突合で振込手数料が帳簿と3万円ほどずれていたことがあります。日付境界の処理漏れが原因で、確定済みデータは上書きせず訂正仕訳を追加して正しました。
c009.java_tx_design: 勘定系の振込サービスで、確定処理に外部与信APIを同期で入れていて、繁忙期にロックが詰まり処理が3分遅延したことがあります。与信照会をトランザクション外に出し、DB更新だけに絞る設計に変えました。ロック待ちは1.5秒から100ms程度まで下がりました。
c009.hiding_and_oncall: 自分の変更が原因の不具合は、その場ですぐ共有します。オンコールは月1回の当番に入っており、後輩のレビューも週1回続けています。育成も自分の仕事だと思っています。

c010.money_correctness: In ClaimsCore, claim payment submissions to our payment processor carry an idempotency key built from claim_id plus a payment attempt sequence number, stored with a unique constraint in a payment_attempts table. About two years ago, a processor-side timeout caused our retry logic to resend a batch of 60 payment requests with a bug in how the sequence number incremented, so 60 requests reused a sequence number that had already succeeded, and our unique constraint silently rejected the retries as duplicates -- which sounds safe, except six of those claims had genuinely different amounts because of a same-day adjustment, and the retries got dropped instead of processed. I found it during weekly reconciliation when six claims showed as paid in our system but the processor showed no matching transaction. I corrected those six manually with new payment entries, not edits to the rejected ones, and fixed the sequence-number bug so it's tied to payment content, not just an incrementing counter.
c010.java_perf_change: Our claim-search endpoint, used heavily by adjusters, sat at p99 of 1.1 seconds against a 400ms target. I measured with a profiler and found we were doing full-text search against Postgres with a trigram index for a field we mostly searched with a leading prefix. My first attempt was adding a Redis cache in front of it, which helped average case but did nothing for p99, since adjusters rarely searched the same claim twice. What worked was switching the index to match the prefix-search pattern we actually used, which took p99 to about 180ms. I kept the old index alongside the new one for a week to compare query plans before dropping it, in case some searches still needed the trigram behavior, which two of them did, so I kept both.
c010.rust_hands_on: In my claims-CSV tool, I got stuck trying to hold a reference to the current row while also building up a Vec of parsed rows to return, and the compiler kept rejecting it because the row reference borrowed from the file reader while I was also trying to own the parsed data long-term. I fixed it by having the parse function return owned String and f64 values immediately instead of holding onto references into the reader's buffer, accepting a small amount of copying I'd been trying to avoid. Separately, I fought a Send issue when I tried to share a running total across a couple of threads using a plain Rc, and switched to an Arc<Mutex<_>> once I understood Rc wasn't thread-safe, which felt obvious in hindsight but took me a confused evening to work out.
c010.incident_response: Around the same period, we had an incident where our adjudication engine's state machine let a claim move from 'approved' straight to 'paid' without passing through a required fraud-review step, for about 45 minutes before I caught it via a mismatch alert on our review-queue depth. Four claims went through that path, totaling around $31,000. I flagged it in our incident channel within ten minutes of noticing, before I'd even confirmed the root cause, paused the affected transition, and had a fix -- a missing state-guard condition -- deployed within two hours. All four claims went through manual fraud review after the fact, and none were found fraudulent, but we still treated it as the process failure it was. The postmortem added an automated test that asserts every terminal state transition passes through its required guard, and I wrote that test myself.
c010.evidence_decision: About three years ago, the team wanted to introduce an event-sourcing model for claim status instead of our current mutable-row-plus-audit-log approach. I disagreed, because I'd measured our audit-log query patterns and found the team mostly needed point-in-time snapshots, which the current model already served in under 50ms, while a naive event-sourcing rebuild in a prototype I built took 300ms plus to reconstruct the same view. The team looked at that prototype and decided to keep the current model but add a proper snapshot table, a middle path I hadn't proposed myself. I built that snapshot table as agreed, and I didn't go back and quietly build the event-sourcing version on my own afterward, even though I still think it would have been technically interesting.
c010.own_contribution: In the state-machine incident, the guard-condition design and the fix were entirely mine -- I found the missing state check, wrote it, and wrote the regression test. What the team did was the fraud re-review of the four affected claims, which I didn't do myself, and the postmortem discussion on whether we needed a stricter escalation policy, which I ended up proposing. For a different example: on the connection-pool fix I described, tracing the thread dumps and deciding to split the reporting job's pool was entirely my own diagnosis, but another engineer wrote the actual pool-configuration change in our deployment manifests from my specification, since that repository wasn't one I had write access to at the time.
c010.rust_boundary: For a ledger-like write path I don't have a production example, but for my claims-CSV tool I did have to decide a boundary of sorts: I kept CSV parsing and validation in Rust, since that's where the tool spends most of its time and where compiler-checked correctness helps most, but I left the eventual write into our reporting database as a separate Python script I already trusted, rather than pulling database access into the Rust side too. What I'd watch in a real production boundary: latency and error rate on the new path, and a running count of any output mismatches against the old path -- the same comparison approach I used to convince myself my Rust totals matched what the old spreadsheet-based process produced before I trusted it.
c010.java_ops: On the same service, we had connection pool exhaustion during month-end reinsurance reporting, when a reporting job ran alongside normal traffic. HikariCP wait time spiked to about 800ms at p95, and normal claim submissions started timing out. I pulled thread dumps during the next occurrence and found the reporting job was holding connections open for the full length of a multi-minute aggregation query instead of releasing them between steps. I rewrote the job to commit and release its connection after each chunk of about 5,000 claims instead of holding one connection for the whole run, and moved it onto a separate 8-connection pool so it couldn't compete with live traffic at all. p95 wait time on the main pool dropped back under 20ms during the next month-end run.
c010.rust_readiness: I don't have production Rust experience. What I have is a couple of personal projects -- the more serious one is a small tool that ingests our claims export CSVs and cross-checks totals, which I rewrote in Rust over a few weekends to force myself past tutorials. I hit real ownership and lifetime problems doing that, which I can go into detail on. My honest view on migrating something like ClaimsCore: I wouldn't propose a full-service rewrite, I'd want to find one boundary that's stateless and easy to verify by comparing outputs against the existing Java path, run both for a while, and only trust the new one once the outputs matched for a sustained period. That's closer to how I'd want to treat any Rust adoption here, given I'm still building real experience rather than claiming production depth I don't have.
c010.process_skipping: Yes, and I'll be honest about it rather than give the tidy answer. During the state-machine incident I just described, I deployed the guard-condition fix myself about ninety minutes in, without waiting for a second reviewer, because claims were actively bypassing fraud review while I waited. I posted in the incident channel right before deploying, not after, saying I was skipping review given active harm, and I logged the diff afterward for the team to review once things were calm. Looking back, I think I could have gotten a one-line ack from anyone online in under two minutes before pushing rather than announcing and going -- the situation didn't actually require skipping that check, just doing it fast, and I've tried to hold myself to a stricter bar since. It's the one time I've done it, and I don't think it was as necessary as it felt in the moment.
c010.prod_data_verification: I've wanted to check a real balance against production more than once, mostly during the sequence-number incident, and what I actually did was take that week's payment_attempts and settlement export, strip claim-holder names and policy numbers, and run my reconciliation query against that masked copy in a scratch database instead of live. For anything I truly couldn't reproduce outside production, like confirming the guard-condition fix actually blocked the bad transition under real traffic timing, I used a read-only query against production that just checked whether any claim had entered the bad state since the fix, without touching or creating any records, and I posted what I was checking in our channel before running it.
c010.java_recovery: After the sequence-number bug I described, I had to restore consistency for the six dropped payments. I scoped it with a query joining payment_attempts against the processor's settlement export for the same date range, which is how I found exactly six mismatches out of about 1,400 payments that week. I fixed each with a new payment_attempts row carrying a corrected sequence number rather than touching the rejected rows, then re-ran our nightly reconciliation job manually against just those six claim IDs to confirm the processor and our system agreed afterward. My first assumption, before I looked closely, was that all 60 rejected retries were affected, not just six; I only narrowed it down once I checked which of the 60 actually had a same-day amount change, which is what protected the other 54 from being real problems.
c010.rust_when_not: I'd hold off moving anything that's still actively changing shape, which in our world is the adjudication engine's state machine -- it's had three real behavior changes in the last year, and a rewrite target needs to sit still long enough to verify against. I haven't held back a full rewrite urge at work, since I've never had production Rust access to even propose one, but on my CSV tool I did hold back from rewriting the reporting-database write step into Rust just because I liked the language, once I noticed the Python script was already fast enough and well-tested; I decided that would have been rewriting for my own enjoyment, not for a real problem.
c010.reconciliation_mismatch: During the same reconciliation cycle where I found the six dropped payments, I separately found a $940 mismatch across the month, all in one direction, unrelated to the sequence-number bug. I traced it to a batch of 8 claims where a late-arriving reinsurance adjustment posted after we'd already closed the month's settlement file, so our internal total moved but the file we'd sent didn't. I corrected it by including those 8 adjustments in the next month's file as their own line items rather than reopening the closed one, and flagged the timing gap to our reinsurance-ops contact so future late adjustments get held for the next cycle instead of landing mid-close. My first read was that it was a rounding issue, since $940 across a large batch looked small enough, and I only found the real cause once I checked timestamps against the file-close time.
c010.java_tx_design: In ClaimsCore, our claims-adjudication service, I once had a transaction that updated a claim's status and then, inside the same @Transactional method, called out to a notification service to email the policyholder. During our nightly batch settlement run, when a few thousand claims move status at once, that external call held the transaction open long enough that other threads updating the same claims table piled up -- I saw over 90 threads blocked on row locks in one run, which pushed batch runtime from 40 minutes to almost two hours. I moved the notification call out of the transaction entirely: the status update commits on its own, and I write a row to an outbox table in the same transaction, which a separate poller picks up to send the email. Batch runtime dropped back under 45 minutes. The failure I didn't foresee at first: the poller could double-send an email if it crashed after sending but before marking the outbox row done, so I added a sent_at check before resending.
c010.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing a mistake: I once shipped a change to claim-amount rounding that was subtly wrong for a specific currency path, and I found it myself two days later while checking something unrelated. I posted about it in our team channel that same afternoon, tagged my manager, and we quantified the impact -- 14 claims, all under $3 difference -- before I'd been asked anything. On-call: I've carried our claims-platform rotation for four years, one week in five, and it's genuinely part of how I think about the job, not separate from it. I also mentor one junior engineer who joined last year, mostly through pairing on incident write-ups, since I think learning to reason about an incident calmly is as much the job as writing the original code.

c011.money_correctness: Every transaction that hits core-ledger carries an idempotency key made of a client-generated request ID plus our internal transaction type, enforced with a unique constraint on a transactions table, and any retried request -- from a client timeout, a mobile app resend, or our own internal retry after a downstream timeout -- gets the original result returned instead of a second debit or credit. This broke for real about two years ago: a partner payment provider we integrate with started retrying webhooks with exponential backoff after a change on our side slowed our webhook handler's acknowledgment past their 3-second timeout, and during a four-hour window before we noticed, roughly 1,200 webhook retries came in. Our idempotency key was built from the provider's own event ID, which we assumed was unique, but it turned out their retries sometimes carried a regenerated event ID after their fifth retry attempt, so 40 of those 1,200 slipped through as duplicate credits totaling about €6,800. We caught it the next morning through our automated reconciliation job comparing our ledger totals against the provider's settlement file. We corrected the 40 duplicates with reversing debit entries, not deletions, and fixed the root cause by keying on the provider's original transaction reference instead of their per-attempt event ID, since that field stayed stable across all of their retries.
c011.java_perf_change: On core-ledger, our account-history endpoint, which customers hit constantly in the mobile app, sat at p99 of 900ms against a target of 250ms once we passed about 400,000 accounts. I measured with a profiler and found the query was doing a full scan across a transactions table partitioned by month, joining across all partitions because our date-range filter wasn't being pushed down properly by our ORM-generated query. My first attempt was adding a covering index on the filtered columns, which helped average latency, roughly 900ms to 500ms, but didn't move p99 much, since the worst-case queries were customers with years of history and no date filter applied. The change that actually worked was adding a default 90-day window on the endpoint with an explicit 'load more' pagination affordance, which is a product change I had to negotiate, not just an engineering one -- most customers never needed more than that anyway, based on usage data I pulled first to justify asking for it. p99 dropped to about 90ms. The side effect: a few high-net-worth customers who did check years of history complained, so we added a separate, explicitly slower 'full history' export path for that minority case instead of optimizing the common path for their needs.
c011.rust_hands_on: In the risk-engine, the ownership problem that took me longest was around our feature cache: I wanted multiple tokio tasks to read from a shared HashMap of recent transaction features while one background task periodically evicted old entries, and my first instinct, coming from Java, was to reach for something like a mutex around the whole map, which worked but serialized every read behind the evictor, killing our latency target under load. I moved to a sharded structure -- effectively several smaller maps each behind their own RwLock, keyed by a hash of the customer ID -- so reads mostly don't contend with each other or with eviction on a different shard. The Send/Sync fight came later, when I tried to share a metrics-reporting closure across tasks that captured a non-Sync type from an early version of our metrics library; the compiler wouldn't let me spawn it across threads, and I spent a confused afternoon before realizing the library had a Sync-safe handle type I wasn't using, exposed under a different name than I expected. On async specifically, an early version of the gRPC handler accidentally held a lock across an .await point during a downstream call, which caused a deadlock under load that took me a day of tokio-console tracing to find, since it only showed up past a certain concurrency level.
c011.incident_response: The clearest incident I've owned end to end is actually the risk-engine memory leak I mentioned. Pods started restarting from OOM kills roughly every six hours, which wasn't originally alarming since Kubernetes just rescheduled them, until the restart frequency climbed to every 40 minutes over about two weeks and each restart caused a brief spike in scoring latency as a fresh pod warmed its caches, pushing p99 above our 10ms budget for a few seconds each time. I got pulled in when an on-call alert fired on sustained p99 breach, traced it with heaptrack over about three hours, and found a feature cache keyed by customer ID that we never evicted, growing unbounded as our customer base grew. I told the team in our incident channel as soon as I had a working theory, not after I'd fixed it, since others needed to know restarts might keep happening for another day while I built the fix. The fix was an LRU eviction policy capped at 500,000 entries, deployed within about six hours of the alert firing. The postmortem's lasting change was a memory-growth alert on all our Rust services, tuned to catch this kind of slow leak in hours instead of weeks; it's caught one other, smaller leak since, in an unrelated service, within about four hours of it starting.
c011.evidence_decision: About four years ago, the team wanted to move core-ledger off Postgres onto a distributed database for horizontal scaling, arguing we'd hit a wall as account count grew. I disagreed, and spent a week benchmarking our actual write throughput against Postgres's documented limits, showing we were using about 8% of a single primary's write capacity even at peak, and that our real growth constraint was the midnight-batch lock contention I described earlier, not raw throughput. I presented that alongside a rough migration-cost estimate, and the team agreed to hold off on the database migration and instead invest in fixing the batch contention, which is the outbox change I made. I didn't quietly keep planning the distributed-database migration on the side; I dropped it entirely once the decision was made, and revisited it three years later, when account growth had actually caught up to a real throughput concern, at which point I was the one who reopened the conversation with new numbers rather than resisting it out of attachment to my earlier position. Separately, I've argued for and lost a case for rewriting a legacy batch-reporting job in Rust for speed, and once the team decided the reporting job wasn't worth the migration risk given how rarely it changes, I maintained it in Java without revisiting that.
c011.own_contribution: In the risk-engine work I described, the parts that were genuinely mine: choosing Rust and the tokio/tonic stack, designing the gRPC boundary and the shadow-traffic comparison period, finding and fixing the memory leak, and the LRU eviction design. What the team did: two other engineers built out the actual feature-lookup data sources the scoring model reads from, which I didn't design, and our data science team owns the scoring model itself -- I just serve it fast and safely, I don't tune its weights. For the core-ledger transaction-boundary work, the diagnosis and the outbox redesign were mine, but the poller-sharding fix I mentioned for the later 5x-traffic problem was actually built by a colleague based on a design doc I wrote, since I was heads-down on the risk-engine leak at the same time. I think it's worth being precise about that distinction, because 'I built the outbox pattern' and 'the team scaled it later' are genuinely different pieces of work, and conflating them would overstate what I personally did on the second half.
c011.rust_boundary: For our risk-engine boundary specifically, I placed it right before core-ledger commits a transaction: core-ledger calls out over gRPC with the transaction's features already assembled, gets back an allow/deny/review decision, and only then proceeds with its own commit. I kept the boundary narrow deliberately -- the Rust service owns scoring and nothing about the ledger's own consistency, so a bug in Rust can reject or approve a transaction but can never corrupt account balances, which live entirely on the Java side. Before migrating, we measured the Java prototype's p99 (45-60ms) and its GC-pause correlation with scoring latency spikes; after the Rust version shipped, we tracked p99 (down to 6ms), error rate, and, for about six weeks, ran the Java and Rust scorers side by side on shadow traffic to compare decisions before letting Rust be authoritative. About 0.3% of transactions disagreed during that shadow period, which we tracked down to a floating-point rounding difference in one feature calculation between the two implementations, and we didn't cut over fully until that gap closed to zero. If I were doing the ledger write path itself rather than a scoring sidecar, I'd apply the same shadow-and-measure approach, but I'd be more conservative about the boundary, since correctness there is much less forgiving of any gap.
c011.java_ops: Operationally, the biggest problem I've owned was GC pauses on our transaction-processing pods once we moved to Kubernetes and started running four replicas under real load. We were on the G1 collector with default settings, and once daily transaction volume passed around two million, we started seeing GC pauses of 800ms to 1.2 seconds roughly every ten minutes, which was enough to trip our p99 latency SLO of 300ms for transfer confirmation. I pulled GC logs with -Xlog:gc and found young-generation collections were the problem, not full GCs, because our heap was undersized relative to allocation rate -- we were allocating a lot of short-lived DTOs per transaction. I increased the young-gen size, from roughly 512MB to 1.5GB of a 4GB heap, and switched our JSON serialization to reuse buffers instead of allocating a new one per request, which cut allocation rate significantly. Pause frequency dropped from every ten minutes to roughly every forty, and p99 pause length came down to under 150ms. It took two rounds to get there -- my first attempt was just raising overall heap size, which didn't help pause frequency and increased full-GC pause length when it did happen, so I reverted that part and focused on generation sizing instead.
c011.rust_readiness: I do have production Rust experience. About three years ago I built and now help run our risk-engine service, which scores every incoming transaction for fraud risk in real time before core-ledger commits it. We chose Rust because the scoring model needs to run in under 10ms at p99 including feature lookups, and our early Java prototype of the same logic was sitting at 45-60ms at p99, mostly from GC pauses interrupting a latency-sensitive hot path we couldn't tolerate pausing. The Rust service uses tokio for the async runtime and tonic for gRPC, talking to core-ledger over a synchronous-feeling request-response call that core-ledger blocks on before committing a transaction. In production it now handles about 300 transactions per second at peak, with p99 around 6ms. The failure I'd point to: about a year in, we had a memory leak from a cache we weren't evicting properly, which grew slowly enough that it took two weeks to show up as pod restarts from OOM kills, and I found it with heaptrack rather than anything obvious in our metrics. My view on migration generally is the same principle that got us here: cut a boundary where there's a real, measured problem, not because the language is more fun to write.
c011.process_skipping: During the OOM-restart incident, once I understood the leak but before I'd fully tested the LRU fix, I was tempted to skip our normal canary rollout and push straight to all pods, since restarts were getting more frequent and I wanted the bleeding to stop. What I actually did was resist that and stick to the procedure: I deployed to one canary pod first, watched its memory curve for about 40 minutes against my prediction, confirmed it was flat where the others were climbing, and only then rolled out to the rest, which added maybe an hour of that pod cycling through a few more restarts than if I'd gone straight to all of them. In hindsight I think that was the right call, because my LRU cap number was a guess, and if it had been wrong I'd have wanted to know that from one pod, not all of them at once. I have skipped procedure exactly once, years earlier at a previous job, during a payment outage, and in hindsight I don't think it was justified -- the outage wasn't getting worse, I was just impatient. The bar I hold myself to now: skip only if measurable harm is actively growing, not just present, and even then announce it and get at least one other set of eyes before deploying, not after.
c011.prod_data_verification: Yes, particularly with the risk-engine's shadow-traffic comparison I described: the honest answer is that comparing real transaction decisions between Java and Rust implementations meant touching real transaction data, and I handled that by making the Rust scorer's decision purely advisory during the shadow period -- it computed a result and logged it, but core-ledger never acted on it, so there was no risk of the comparison itself affecting a real customer, even though the underlying data was live and real. For situations where I couldn't get away with even that, like verifying the interest-accrual idempotency fix under real concurrent load rather than staging's much lower traffic, I used a masked copy of a weekend's real transaction volume replayed against a staging environment scaled to match production concurrency, rather than testing against live accounts. I have, once, checked a single live account balance directly, during the interest-accrual incident, to confirm my hypothesis about the average overpayment before writing the correction script, and I posted the specific account ID I was checking in our incident channel along with why, rather than treating it as routine. I don't think occasional, announced, read-only checks against production are the same as using production as a general test environment, but I do try to keep the bar for doing even that fairly high.
c011.java_recovery: Beyond the webhook-duplicate incident, there was an earlier case, about five years ago, where a bug in our interest-accrual batch job double-applied interest to about 900 savings accounts over a weekend because the job wasn't idempotent against being re-run after a partial failure -- it crashed halfway through Saturday's run, and our on-call at the time just reran it Sunday without checking which accounts had already been processed. I scoped the damage by comparing each account's accrual-log entries against expected entries for that date range, which is how I got the 900 number and confirmed the average overpayment was about €4.10 per account, small individually but real. I corrected it with a reversing accrual entry for each account, dated to the correction date rather than backdated, and I built a lock-based idempotency check into the batch job itself so a rerun would skip any account already processed for that date. I verified the fix by re-running the job against a full copy of that weekend's data in staging and confirming zero double-applications, then verified in production by re-checking accrual totals against expected interest for the next three weekends after the fix shipped, since I wanted more than one clean run before I trusted it.
c011.rust_when_not: I wouldn't move our account-history endpoint or most of core-ledger's account-facing read paths to Rust, even though they're the most customer-visible code we have, because they change constantly as product requirements shift and the team maintaining them is Java-focused; a rewrite there would trade measured performance for a maintenance burden nobody currently owns. I did hold back a real urge once: after the risk-engine's success, I wanted to also rewrite our legacy fraud-rules engine, an older rule-based system that runs alongside the newer model-based scorer, in Rust for consistency's sake. When I actually measured it, its p99 was 4ms with no real latency budget pressure, and its main cost was engineering time to maintain rule changes, which our fraud team, not engineers, edits through a simple DSL -- rewriting it in Rust would have meant either losing that DSL editability or rebuilding it, for a system with no performance problem. I raised the idea, measured it honestly in front of the team, and dropped it once the numbers didn't support it, rather than building a prototype first to make the case emotionally. My criteria generally: is there a real, measured latency or reliability problem, and does the team that owns the code's future changes actually want to own it in the new language.
c011.reconciliation_mismatch: Beyond the webhook-duplicate case, there was a settlement mismatch about three years ago where our daily reconciliation against a card-network settlement file showed we were short by about €2,300 across roughly 15,000 transactions for the day, which is small in aggregate but I don't like unexplained gaps regardless of size. I traced it by bucketing the mismatch by transaction hour and found it clustered entirely around 11 p.m., which lined up with the card network's own day-boundary cutoff sitting in a different timezone than ours; about 30 transactions near midnight our time landed in the network's 'next day' settlement file instead of the one we expected, so they appeared to us as missing for a day and then reappeared the next day as an apparent surplus. Once I understood it was a timing artifact rather than a real loss, I corrected our reconciliation logic to bucket by the network's day boundary instead of ours, rather than touching any actual ledger entries, since nothing was actually wrong with the money, only with how we were comparing it. My first hypothesis, before I found the timezone issue, was a rounding difference in currency conversion, since that's the more common cause I'd seen before, and I spent a wasted afternoon on that theory before checking timestamps.
c011.java_tx_design: At the neobank, our core-ledger service does double-entry bookkeeping: every transfer between accounts must write a debit and a credit row atomically, and for years we wrapped that write together with a call to our notification service inside one Spring transaction, since it was simple and worked fine while we had under 50,000 accounts. As we grew past 400,000 accounts, our midnight standing-order batch, which processes maybe 60,000 transfers in a ten-minute window, started showing serious lock contention on the account_balances table -- I traced it with Postgres's pg_locks view and found transactions were held open for 200-400ms because the notification call inside them was slow and occasionally retried. My decision was to shrink the transaction to only the debit and credit write, which must stay atomic together for correctness, and move the notification into an outbox table written in the same transaction, drained by a separate poller. Lock hold time dropped to under 15ms. The failure that followed: under a later 5x traffic spike, the outbox poller itself became a bottleneck and fell eight minutes behind, so customers got transfer notifications late; I fixed that by sharding the poller by account-id range instead of running it single-threaded.
c011.hiding_and_oncall: On sharing early: about a year ago I pushed a config change to the risk-engine's feature-lookup timeout that I thought was safe, and it quietly increased our false-decline rate by roughly 0.4 percentage points for eleven hours before a product manager noticed customer complaints ticking up. Once I traced it back to my change, I posted in our incident channel within fifteen minutes of confirming it, named it as my mistake specifically rather than 'a regression,' and we estimated the number of wrongly declined transactions -- about 340 -- so support could reach out proactively. On-call and mentoring: I've carried on-call for the risk-engine and core-ledger, combined, for about six years across two companies, one week in four currently, and I still take pages myself rather than routing everything to whoever's more junior. I mentor two engineers who joined in the last year, one of whom I'm walking through their first on-call rotation next month, shadowing with me first. I don't think of any of this as beneath the work of designing systems; the on-call load is exactly what tells me whether a design decision I made was actually a good one once it meets real traffic, so I'd trust my own design judgment less if I'd stopped carrying a pager.

c012.money_correctness: On TaxCore, every refund disbursement carries an idempotency key made from the taxpayer's filing ID plus the tax year, enforced with a unique constraint in a disbursements table, so a retried disbursement request after a timeout returns the existing record instead of issuing a second payment. This broke about three years ago: our payment processor's callback endpoint started timing out under load during a surge, and our retry logic resent 85 disbursement requests over about five hours with a bug that generated a new filing-ID-plus-year key each time, due to a data-type mismatch in how the tax year was formatted between two of our internal services. I found it during our weekly reconciliation, which showed 85 taxpayers with two disbursement records instead of one, totaling about $142,000 in duplicate payments. I corrected each with a reversing entry, not a deletion, and fixed the formatting mismatch so key generation was consistent across both services.
c012.java_perf_change: Our return-status lookup endpoint, which taxpayers hit through the public portal, sat at p99 of 1.8 seconds during filing season against a target of 500ms. I measured with a profiler and found we were doing a join across three tables for every lookup when only one was actually needed for the common case of checking status, the others were pulled for an edit-history feature almost nobody used on that screen. My first attempt was caching the whole response, which helped average latency but did little for p99, since most lookups were for accounts filed within the last day and rarely repeated. What worked was splitting the query so the common status-only case skipped the two unused joins entirely, dropping p99 to about 240ms. I kept the full query available behind a separate, explicit endpoint for the edit-history feature so I wasn't removing functionality, just not paying its cost on every request.
c012.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust code, production or personal, so I don't have a real answer here beyond saying so plainly. I've read a bit about ownership and the borrow checker out of general interest, but I haven't sat down and actually hit a compiler error myself, which I think is a meaningfully different thing from having done it.
c012.incident_response: Separately, we had an incident where a batch job that applies interest to overdue tax balances ran twice for the same night because a scheduler misconfiguration after a deployment left two scheduled triggers active instead of one. It affected about 6,000 accounts with double-applied interest, averaging $3.20 extra per account. I noticed it the next morning from an anomaly in our daily accrual-total dashboard, which showed roughly double the expected interest applied, and had the affected account list scoped by 10 a.m. and a reversing-entry fix deployed by 2 p.m. the same day. I told my lead and our operations contact as soon as I suspected the double-run, before I'd finished scoping it, since taxpayer-facing statements go out the next day and needed to be held. The postmortem's change was adding a check at job startup that fails loudly if another instance is already running, which we verified by intentionally triggering a double-run in staging afterward.
c012.evidence_decision: About two years ago, a colleague proposed rewriting our refund-calculation module from scratch, arguing the existing code was too hard to follow. I disagreed with a full rewrite and instead pulled our incident history, showing we'd had exactly one bug in that module in three years, plus an estimate of the two to three months a rewrite would take against other backlog work. The team discussed it and decided against the full rewrite, opting instead for me to refactor the module's worst-documented section incrementally over a few weeks while leaving the rest alone. I did that refactor as agreed and didn't go back and quietly rewrite the rest of it afterward, even though I still think parts of it could be cleaner, because the team's call was that the risk of a rewrite wasn't worth it for code that wasn't actually causing problems.
c012.own_contribution: In the disbursement idempotency-key fix I described, tracing the formatting mismatch between the two services and designing the corrected key format was my own work; a colleague on the payments-integration side implemented the change on their service's end once I'd specified what the key needed to look like. For the scheduler-duplication incident, scoping the 6,000 affected accounts and writing the reversing-entry logic was mine; the actual startup-check code that prevents a future double-run was written by another engineer on my team from a short design note I wrote, since he was already deep in that part of the codebase and could move faster than I could there. I think it's worth naming that split rather than saying 'we fixed it,' since the diagnosis and the fix design were mine specifically, and the implementation of the prevention measure wasn't.
c012.rust_boundary: Without Rust experience myself, I'd still apply the same approach I used moving the audit-flagging call out of our transaction: find the least stateful, most isolated piece of the write path first, something like fee or interest calculation that takes inputs and returns a number without needing to touch the database directly, and put that behind an interface the Java side calls. I'd run it in parallel with the existing Java calculation for some weeks, logging both results, and only cut over once outputs matched consistently. What I'd watch: latency of the new call, error rate, and a count of any mismatches against the Java result. I don't have my own experience carving this particular kind of boundary in Rust, so I'd want a more experienced Rust engineer to sanity-check the interface design before I trusted my own judgment on it fully.
c012.java_ops: We had connection pool exhaustion on the same service during that same March surge, before I made the transaction fix. HikariCP wait times hit 900ms at p95, and I pulled pool metrics from Grafana showing all 25 connections were in use for stretches of 2-3 seconds at a time, correlated with the slow audit calls I mentioned. Before I understood the root cause, my first move was just raising pool size from 25 to 50, which briefly helped the wait metric but pushed our database's own connection limit close to its ceiling of 200 total across all services, so I reverted that within a day. The actual fix was the transaction-boundary change, which reduced how long connections were held per request; after that, pool wait dropped to under 30ms at p95 even at the same peak volume, without needing more connections at all.
c012.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust, in production or otherwise, so I want to be upfront about that rather than talk around it. If I were building a realistic plan, I'd start with the official book and Rustlings over the first month, alongside rewriting something small I already understand well -- probably our refund-calculation logic, since I know its edge cases from having built it in Java -- to force myself to hit ownership and borrowing for real. I'd expect the first two months to be mostly fighting the compiler on things that are simple in Java, and I wouldn't feel ready to own a production boundary until I'd built at least one real async service end to end, maybe four to six months in. On migration generally, I'd want to move a small, stateless, well-tested piece first and run it alongside the Java version rather than trust a rewrite immediately, which is closer to how I approach any risky change, language aside.
c012.process_skipping: During the interest-double-application incident, I was tempted to skip the normal review step and push the scheduler fix immediately once I found it, since statements were going out that evening. I didn't skip it: I posted in our team channel, got a colleague to review the one-line scheduler config change over a ten-minute call instead of our usual next-day review cycle, and got it merged and deployed within that window. I think the key thing that made review possible even under time pressure was that the fix itself was small and easy to reason about quickly, which isn't always true. I'd only consider actually skipping review if getting even a fast second opinion were genuinely impossible and real harm were actively accumulating, and I'd want to announce that decision and log it clearly rather than quietly doing it and explaining later, which I haven't personally had to do.
c012.prod_data_verification: I've wanted to check something against real production balances more than once, most clearly during the disbursement duplicate-payment issue, and what I did was take that week's disbursements and filing records, strip taxpayer names and account numbers, and run my grouping query against that masked copy in a separate database rather than live. For the scheduler-duplication incident, where I needed to confirm the startup check actually prevented a second run under real conditions, I tested that in staging by deliberately triggering a duplicate scheduler trigger there, rather than trying to reproduce it in production at all. The one time I checked a live number directly was confirming the $3.20-per-account average from the interest incident, which I did with a read-only query and mentioned in our incident channel before running it, since I wanted the number for the postmortem rather than to change anything.
c012.java_recovery: The 85-disbursement duplicate-payment issue is my clearest recovery example. I scoped it with a query joining disbursements against filing_id and tax_year, grouping to find any pair with matching taxpayer and year but different disbursement IDs, which is how I got the exact count of 85 and confirmed the $142,000 total. For each one I checked the payment processor's own transaction log to be sure both payments had actually gone out, since I didn't want to assume every flagged pair was a real duplicate. I fixed each with a reversing disbursement entry dated to the discovery date, then re-ran our weekly reconciliation manually against just those 85 filing IDs afterward to confirm balances matched. My first assumption was that the bug affected any retried disbursement, but once I checked timestamps I found it only hit requests retried during that specific five-hour window when the callback timeouts were happening, which narrowed the blast radius considerably.
c012.rust_when_not: Without hands-on Rust experience, I'd still say I wouldn't move anything that's actively changing or poorly understood by the team maintaining it, since a rewrite needs stability to verify against, and our own team is entirely Java-focused right now. On holding back a rewrite urge specifically in Rust, I don't have that experience, but I have held back a rewrite urge in Java: I wanted to rewrite our refund-calculation module, which I described in the evidence-decision question, and the team's data on incident history convinced me it wasn't worth the risk. I think the same reasoning would apply to a Rust rewrite if I were ever tempted -- measure whether there's a real problem first, rather than assume a new language would fix something that isn't actually broken.
c012.reconciliation_mismatch: During a quarterly reconciliation about two years ago, our totals were off by $890 across roughly 3,000 refund disbursements for the quarter, small per-account but consistent enough that I didn't write it off as noise. I traced it to how we handled partial refunds for taxpayers who'd filed an amended return after their original refund had already gone out -- the amendment logic recalculated the full refund amount and disbursed the difference, but for eleven cases a second amendment arrived before the first amendment's disbursement had settled, so the second amendment's calculation was based on stale data. I corrected those eleven with adjusting entries based on recalculating from the final settled state, not the intermediate one, and added a check that blocks a new amendment calculation from starting until the prior one's disbursement confirms as settled. My first guess was a currency-rounding issue, since $890 across 3,000 looked small enough to be that, and I ruled it out only after checking each case's timeline individually.
c012.java_tx_design: On our tax-assessment service, I ran into a boundary problem processing refund calculations. Originally the whole assessment -- validate the return, compute the refund, write the refund record, and call our internal audit-flagging service -- ran in one @Transactional method. During the March filing surge, when we process about 40,000 returns a day instead of the usual 5,000, transactions blocked on the same taxpayer_accounts row for up to 600ms whenever the audit-flagging call was slow. I moved the audit call outside the transaction: the assessment and refund write commit together, since those two must be atomic, and I write a queued 'needs audit check' row in the same transaction instead of calling out synchronously. Assessment latency at p99 dropped from about 1.4 seconds to 220ms during peak. The failure I hit afterward: the audit queue itself backed up 3,000 rows deep during one surge because I hadn't sized its consumer for peak volume, so I added a second consumer instance.
c012.hiding_and_oncall: I once shipped a rounding change to how we calculate late-payment penalties that was technically correct but changed the result for about 200 existing draft assessments in a way I hadn't checked before deploying. I found the discrepancy myself the next day while spot-checking an unrelated ticket, and reported it to my lead that same afternoon along with the affected count, rather than waiting to see if anyone else noticed first. On on-call: I've been on our rotation for about five years, one week in six, and I handle taxpayer-facing incident escalations directly rather than just paging someone else. I also mentor one junior engineer currently, mostly through code review and walking through incidents like the scheduler one together after the fact, and I've never seen on-call or that kind of mentoring time as separate from the actual engineering work.

c013.money_correctness: At my company, we had processes in place to make sure payments weren't duplicated, generally using some kind of key to identify each request so that retries wouldn't cause the same charge to happen twice. We also had reconciliation processes that ran regularly to catch anything that looked off. I understand the general approach -- idempotency keys, retry handling, and periodic checks -- but I wasn't the one designing those systems, and I didn't personally handle an incident where something went wrong with them. It was more something the team maintained collectively.
c013.java_perf_change: We worked on performance improvements from time to time, generally looking at what seemed to be running slowly and trying different things to speed it up. I helped test some of these changes and confirm things seemed better afterward, but I wasn't usually the one doing the actual profiling or deciding what to change first. I don't have specific numbers to share since I wasn't tracking the metrics directly myself, that was mostly something the senior engineers on the team looked at.
c013.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust code, so I don't have an example of getting stuck on something like ownership or lifetimes to share. It's something I'd expect to run into once I actually started writing real code in it, but I can't speak to it from experience yet.
c013.incident_response: We had incidents from time to time, and generally the process was to figure out what caused it, fix it, and then look back afterward to see what could be improved. I was involved in some of these as part of the team, mostly helping out where I could, but I wasn't usually the one leading the investigation or making the key decisions during the response. Afterward we'd usually have a retrospective meeting to talk about what happened and what we could do differently, though I don't remember the specifics of any one incident in detail.
c013.evidence_decision: There have been times I disagreed with a technical decision the team made, and generally I'd raise my concerns in a meeting or a chat and see what others thought. Sometimes the team went a different direction than what I suggested, and in those cases I went along with the decision and helped implement it rather than pushing back further afterward. I think it's important to voice disagreement early but also to accept the outcome once a decision has actually been made, even if I'm not fully convinced.
c013.own_contribution: That's fair -- looking back at what I said about the transaction-boundary work, I think my role was mostly implementing changes that had already been discussed and agreed on by the more senior members of the team, rather than making the underlying design decisions myself. For the incident-response side of things, I'd say something similar: I helped out where I could, following along with what others were doing, but I couldn't point to a specific piece that was entirely my own call. I think I'm still building up to owning that kind of decision on my own.
c013.rust_boundary: I don't have direct experience deciding where to place a boundary like that. Generally I think you'd want to be careful and start with something that isn't too critical, and make sure whatever you changed still matched up with what the rest of the system expected. I imagine you'd want to keep an eye on things like performance and correctness before and after, but I haven't been part of a project that actually did this kind of migration, so I can't speak to it from real experience.
c013.java_ops: We did run into some performance issues from time to time, generally related to how the JVM or the connection pool was configured. The senior engineers usually handled the actual tuning, looking at various metrics and dashboards to figure out what needed adjusting. I was involved in some of the discussions and helped test changes afterward, but I wasn't the one driving the investigation or making the final call on what to change. I think learning it would involve getting comfortable with how it handles memory differently from Java, and I'd probably start with some general online resources to get familiar with the basics before trying to apply it to anything real. I don't have a concrete plan yet for how long that would take or exactly where I'd start, since I haven't looked into it in enough depth to say.
c013.process_skipping: I don't think I've personally been in a situation where I had to decide whether to skip review or the normal deployment process. Generally the team took the position that you should follow the process even under pressure, and that's the approach I'd want to take too. I think skipping steps should only happen in genuinely serious situations, and even then it should be something the team knows about, not just a personal decision made quietly. But I haven't had to actually make that call myself.
c013.prod_data_verification: I don't think I've personally felt tempted to check something using production data directly. Generally the approach on my team was to use other methods, like a copy of the data or some kind of test environment, when something couldn't easily be verified otherwise. I think that's the right way to handle it, even if I haven't had to make that particular judgment call myself in a real situation.
c013.java_recovery: We did have situations where data needed to be corrected after something went wrong, and generally the approach was to figure out what was affected and fix it carefully rather than rushing. I was involved in some of that work, mostly helping verify things afterward, but I wasn't usually the one leading the investigation into what had actually broken or deciding exactly how to fix it. It's an area where I've mostly supported more senior engineers rather than driven the process myself.

I haven't been part of a decision like that myself, so I can't point to a specific example of holding back a rewrite, but that's the general principle I'd expect to follow -- only make a change like that if there's an actual reason to.
c013.reconciliation_mismatch: We did have situations where numbers didn't quite match during reconciliation, and generally the team would look into what caused the difference, whether it was timing, rounding, or something else, and correct it appropriately. I was aware of these situations happening and understood the general approach to fixing them, but I wasn't usually the one who tracked down the exact cause or made the correction myself. It was more something handled by others on the team with more experience in that area.
c013.java_tx_design: I've worked with transaction boundaries in Java services, generally keeping things consistent so that related updates happen together. On the team I was part of, we generally discussed where boundaries should go, and I helped implement some of what was decided. I don't remember a specific incident where it became a big problem, but we were always careful about making sure transactions didn't get too large or hold things open longer than necessary. It's something the more senior engineers on the team usually took the lead on deciding, and I mostly followed their guidance and implemented accordingly.
c013.hiding_and_oncall: I try to be upfront when something goes wrong that I was involved in, generally letting the relevant people know as soon as I'm aware of it rather than waiting. I've done some on-call and handled various support requests as part of my role, and I think that kind of work is a normal part of being on a team, not something separate from the real engineering work. I haven't had much opportunity to mentor anyone yet, since I'm still fairly early in my own career, but I'd expect to take that on eventually.

c014.money_correctness: I don't have experience with idempotency keys or payment reconciliation -- nothing in my background has touched money-handling systems. What I've dealt with that rhymes with it is message deduplication over an unreliable CAN bus link between two boards, where a retried command could arrive twice if an acknowledgment got dropped. I added a sequence number to each command frame and had the receiving board track the last few sequence numbers it had already executed in a small ring buffer, so a duplicate retry got acknowledged again but not re-executed. We found this mattered after a field unit re-triggered a motor-calibration routine twice from a single button press because of exactly this kind of duplicate delivery, which we caught from a customer report and reproduced on the bench with an injected duplicate frame.
c014.java_perf_change: I don't have a Java performance-tuning story, but I've done the equivalent on firmware: our sensor-fusion loop was taking about 1.8ms per cycle against a 1ms budget on a 1kHz control loop, which meant we were occasionally missing cycles. I profiled it using cycle counters on the microcontroller and found a trigonometric function call, computed with the standard library's full-precision implementation, was eating almost half the cycle budget for a case where we didn't need full precision. My first attempt was a lookup table, which got us to 1.1ms but introduced visible quantization error in the output. What worked was a CORDIC-based approximation tuned to our actual precision needs, which got the loop down to 0.6ms with no meaningful accuracy loss, verified against a reference implementation over a large batch of recorded sensor traces.
c014.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust code, so I don't have a real ownership or lifetime story from it. The nearest thing I can offer is a memory-safety bug I did chase down in C, which is part of why I find Rust's guarantees appealing in theory: a use-after-free in our sensor-fusion module where a pointer to a buffer got cached before the buffer was reallocated on a configuration change, causing a rare crash that only showed up after several hours of runtime. I found it with a combination of a heap sanitizer running on a desktop simulation build of the firmware and manually reasoning through every place that buffer pointer was captured. It's exactly the class of bug I understand Rust's borrow checker would have caught at compile time, though I'm speaking about that from the outside, not from having used Rust myself.
c014.incident_response: I haven't operated a production backend system, so I don't have that kind of incident to describe. The incident I know in detail from the inside is the calibration-corruption issue I mentioned earlier: it started showing up as intermittent field returns over about four months before we connected it to the flash-write timing problem, since each unit failed differently depending on exactly when the interrupt landed. Once I had a hypothesis, I built a fault-injection rig that fired a simulated CAN interrupt at a swept range of timings during a flash write, which reproduced the corruption reliably within about an hour of testing instead of waiting days for a field report. I wrote up the timeline and the fix in our internal failure-review process, and the double-buffered flash layout I described is what came out of that review, plus a new bench test that runs the fault-injection sweep on every board revision before it ships.
c014.evidence_decision: I don't have a Java-team technical-decision story, but I have a firmware one: I disagreed with a decision to switch our sensor-fusion filter from a fixed-point implementation to floating-point, arguing it would hurt performance on our Cortex-M4 without an FPU. I benchmarked both on the actual target hardware, showing the floating-point version took about 3.5 times longer per filter update using the compiler's soft-float library, which would have blown our timing budget. The team looked at those numbers and kept fixed-point. I didn't go back and quietly prototype the floating-point version afterward to prove a point; I did help design a better fixed-point scaling scheme instead, which addressed the precision concern that had motivated the original proposal in the first place.
c014.own_contribution: Since I don't have Java experience, I'll apply this to the calibration-corruption fix I described. The parts that were mine specifically: identifying the interrupt-timing root cause, building the fault-injection rig, and designing the double-buffered flash layout. What the team did: another engineer implemented the checksum-verification code that confirms a buffer swap is safe, working from a spec I wrote, and our test lead built the automated bench test that now runs the fault-injection sweep on every board revision, which wasn't something I built myself even though I proposed it in the failure review. I think that's a fair split to name, since the diagnosis and design were mine but two other people built real pieces of the eventual solution.
c014.rust_boundary: I don't have a ledger or Java-to-Rust migration to speak to directly. The closest decision I've made is choosing what to isolate onto a separate microcontroller entirely, rather than a separate language, on a multi-board sensor system: we split the time-critical motor-control loop onto its own dedicated MCU running a tight 1kHz control loop in C, communicating over SPI with a second MCU that handled the higher-level logging, Bluetooth reporting, and configuration, which could tolerate more jitter. Before splitting it, the shared single-MCU version was missing its control deadline about 2% of the time under heavy logging load; after the split, the control loop hit its deadline essentially always, verified over a week of continuous bench testing with a deadline-miss counter. I think about a service boundary the same way I thought about that hardware split: isolate what has a hard real-time or correctness requirement from what doesn't.
c014.java_ops: I don't have Java operational experience -- no GC tuning, no connection pools, nothing on Kubernetes. My closest experience is tuning interrupt priorities and stack sizes on an ARM Cortex-M4 running FreeRTOS for an industrial sensor board. We had a watchdog reset happening roughly once every two or three days in the field, and I traced it, using a logic analyzer and the chip's fault status registers, to a lower-priority sensor-polling task starving a higher-priority safety-check task during bursts of CAN traffic. I restructured the task priorities and added a hard 2ms budget to the polling task using the RTOS's tick-based preemption, measured with a scope on a GPIO toggle at the start and end of each task run. Watchdog resets dropped to about one every four months after that, and the remaining ones turned out to be a separate hardware issue with a marginal oscillator on one board revision.
c014.rust_readiness: I haven't worked with production Rust or thought seriously about a Java-to-Rust migration, since my background isn't in Java at all. Where I have thought hard about language-level safety tradeoffs is in firmware: on my current board we debated whether to write a new sensor-fusion module in C or in a safer subset like MISRA-C with static analysis, given how expensive a memory-safety bug is when it's running on hardware in the field with no easy way to patch it. We ended up sticking with C plus a heavier static-analysis and code-review process, mostly because our whole toolchain -- the debugger, the RTOS, the bootloader -- was already built around it, and rewriting the toolchain integration felt riskier than the bug class we were trying to avoid. That experience of weighing a language change against integration risk is the closest thing I have to an opinion here, even though it wasn't Rust.
c014.process_skipping: I don't have Java deploy-procedure experience, but firmware has its own version of this: our release process requires two engineers to sign off on any change that touches the bootloader or flash-write path, since a bad bootloader update can brick a device in the field with no recovery path. During the calibration-corruption incident, I was tempted to push my double-buffering fix straight to a batch of returned field units without the usual second sign-off, since customers were waiting. I didn't skip it -- I got a colleague to review the flash-layout change specifically, even on a compressed same-day timeline, because a bootloader-adjacent mistake there is much harder to undo than most other bugs I've caused, and I think that kind of asymmetric cost is exactly when a review step matters most, not least.
c014.prod_data_verification: I don't have production-balance or money-data verification experience. The nearest equivalent I've faced is being tempted to test a firmware change directly on field-returned units rather than only in the lab, since some intermittent bugs, including the flash-corruption issue, only showed up under real field conditions I couldn't fully reproduce on the bench. What I actually did was build the fault-injection rig I described instead of experimenting on customer-owned hardware, and only tested against units that had already been returned as defective and taken out of service, never against units still active in the field. When I truly couldn't reproduce something on the bench, I'd request a small number of decommissioned field units through our returns process rather than push an unverified change to anything still in customer hands.
c014.java_recovery: I haven't restored data consistency in a Java service, since I haven't worked on one. The closest experience is recovering corrupted calibration data on field units after the flash-write bug I described: I wrote a recovery tool that read each affected unit's flash sector over JTAG, checked it against a checksum, and if corrupted, restored it from a factory-default calibration table stored in a separate, write-protected flash region, then flagged that unit for a full recalibration on its next service visit. Across the field units we could reach, 23 out of a batch of 40 returned units had corrupted calibration data; I confirmed each recovery worked by reading the sector back and re-verifying its checksum, then running the unit through our standard calibration-verification test before marking it fixed.
c014.rust_when_not: I don't have a Rust-versus-Java rewrite decision to describe, but I've been part of a similar debate about whether to port our RTOS-based firmware to a from-scratch bare-metal design for better determinism. I argued against a full rewrite, since our current RTOS-based system, measured over months of field data, was missing its 1kHz control deadline only about 0.1% of the time, which we'd already addressed for the worst offenders with the task-priority fix I mentioned earlier. A full bare-metal rewrite would have meant redoing years of validated driver code for a problem that was already mostly solved. We kept the RTOS and instead moved the two most timing-sensitive tasks I described onto their own dedicated core, which is the more surgical version of the same idea I'd apply to any full-rewrite temptation.
c014.reconciliation_mismatch: I don't have settlement or reconciliation experience from a money-handling system. The closest analog I've worked on is verifying that a batch of manufactured units' calibration data matched what our test station recorded at the factory, after a field audit found seven units, out of a batch of 500, reporting calibration values that didn't match their factory test record. I traced it to a firmware update pushed between manufacturing and the audit that silently reset one calibration field to a default value under a specific startup condition involving a low-battery boot. I corrected the seven units by re-flashing them from their preserved factory test records rather than guessing at the value, and added a startup check that refuses to apply that default reset if a valid calibration record is already present in flash.
c014.java_tx_design: I haven't worked on a production Java backend, so I don't have a transaction boundary story from that world. What I have dealt with is something adjacent in spirit: on an automotive ECU I worked on, we had a similar problem with critical sections around flash writes for calibration data. Writing a new calibration table took about 40ms, and if a CAN bus interrupt fired mid-write and tried to read the same flash sector, you'd get a corrupted read. I redesigned the write routine to use a double-buffered flash layout instead of writing in place, so interrupts always read a fully-committed buffer while a background task prepared the next one, then atomically swapped a single pointer once the new buffer was verified with a checksum. It cut our field-reported calibration-corruption incidents from about six a year to zero over the following eighteen months, which is the part of that work I'm proudest of.
c014.hiding_and_oncall: I don't have Java-world on-call experience, but our firmware team runs something similar: a rotation for triaging field-device returns and CAN-bus diagnostic logs, which I've done for about a year and a half, roughly one week in four. On sharing a mistake: I once flashed a test board with a debug build that had verbose logging left on, which filled its flash log partition within days and caused it to silently stop recording new faults; I found this myself checking an unrelated board and reported it to my lead the same day, since it meant a batch of field-test boards might have gaps in their fault history. I also mentor one intern currently, mostly on debugging with a logic analyzer and reading datasheets carefully, and I don't think of triaging returned hardware as less important than writing new firmware -- it's usually where I learn what I actually got wrong.

c015.money_correctness: Every payout in our system carries an idempotency key built from seller_id, payout_batch_id, and a payout sequence number, enforced with a unique constraint on the payouts table. About eighteen months ago, we had a batch worker crash partway through a run due to an unrelated infrastructure issue, and our restart logic reran the batch from the beginning instead of resuming from where it left off, because the resume-checkpoint logic had a bug that only triggered on that specific crash type. That resent 2,100 payout requests that had already succeeded. Our idempotency key caught almost all of them, but 19 payouts slipped through as duplicates because their sequence numbers had been assigned before the crash but the payouts table row confirming success hadn't committed yet, so the retry saw no existing row and proceeded, totaling about £7,400 in double payouts. We caught it the next morning via our daily bank-statement reconciliation. We corrected the 19 with reversing ledger entries and fixed the resume logic to check the bank's own transfer confirmation, not just our local row, before deciding whether a payout needed to be resent.
c015.java_perf_change: Our seller-payout-history endpoint, which sellers check constantly through our partner dashboard, sat at p99 of 2.1 seconds against a 500ms target once a seller had more than a couple of years of payout history. I profiled it and found we were recalculating currency-converted totals on every request instead of storing them, doing a live rate lookup for every historical payout row even though historical rates never change once a payout settles. My first attempt was caching the whole response per seller, which helped average case but barely touched p99, since long-tenured sellers rarely hit cache with fresh data anyway. What actually worked was storing the converted total at settlement time as a column on the payout row itself, so historical rows never needed a live rate lookup again, only new payouts did. p99 dropped to about 140ms. The migration to backfill that column for historical rows took a weekend batch job I ran manually, watching it against a staging copy first since a mistake there would have meant showing sellers the wrong historical totals.
c015.rust_hands_on: In the currency-conversion tool I mentioned, I got stuck trying to build a struct that held a reference to the 'current' exchange-rate table while a separate update thread periodically replaced that table wholesale with a freshly-fetched one. The compiler rejected my first attempt because I was trying to hold a long-lived reference into data that could be dropped out from under it whenever the update thread swapped tables. I fixed it with an Arc<RwLock<RateTable>>, so readers clone a fresh Arc to get a consistent snapshot at the moment they read, and the update thread swaps the whole table under a write lock without invalidating anyone already holding a snapshot. It took me a couple of evenings to understand why my first instinct, a plain reference, couldn't work here, and honestly it mapped pretty directly onto a problem I'd already solved differently in Java with a volatile reference swap, which is part of why it finally clicked.
c015.incident_response: Separate from the duplicate-payout issue, we had an incident where a bug in our currency-rate cache -- the same one from the memory-leak story, actually, before I'd fixed the leak -- served a stale GBP/EUR rate that was about six hours old during a period where the rate had moved meaningfully, affecting roughly 400 seller payouts converted at the wrong rate, undercutting sellers by an average of £2.80 each. I noticed it from a seller-support escalation, not an internal alert, which was itself a gap I flagged in the postmortem. I scoped the affected payouts within about 90 minutes by cross-referencing our rate-cache logs against the real historical rate feed, and we issued corrective top-up payments to all 400 sellers within 24 hours, calculated individually rather than as a flat estimate. The postmortem's lasting change was adding an internal alert on rate-cache staleness beyond 15 minutes, which is what would have caught this before a customer did.
c015.evidence_decision: About four years ago, the team debated whether to move seller balances to an eventually-consistent replicated store to improve read availability during regional outages. I argued against it, using six months of our own uptime data showing our single-region Postgres primary had 99.97% availability, well above what the added complexity of eventual consistency would buy us, against a rough estimate that reconciling eventual-consistency conflicts on money balances would cost significant engineering time we didn't have budgeted. The team agreed to hold off and instead invest in faster primary failover, which is what we built. I didn't quietly prototype the replicated-store version afterward; two years later, when we expanded into a second region and the calculus genuinely changed, I was the one who reopened that conversation with new numbers, rather than resurrecting my old preference out of attachment to it.
c015.own_contribution: In the escrow-release transaction-boundary work I described, the diagnosis and the redesign into a fast-commit-plus-async-reconciliation pattern were entirely mine. What the team did: another engineer built the reconciliation job that compares provisional and confirmed withholding estimates, from a spec I wrote, since I was focused on the batch-worker changes at the same time. For the stale-rate incident, scoping the 400 affected payouts and designing the correction approach was my work; calculating and issuing the actual top-up payments was done by our finance-ops team using a script I wrote but didn't run myself, since they own the actual disbursement step for corrections, not engineering. I think that distinction matters -- I designed and built the tool, they made the call on which payments to send and confirmed each one.
c015.rust_boundary: If I were moving part of our payout-batch write path, I'd start with the withholding-estimate calculation, not the escrow release or the actual fund transfer. It's pure computation given a payout amount, a seller's tax jurisdiction, and a rate table, no database writes of its own beyond logging the result. I'd put it behind an interface the Java batch worker calls, run both implementations against every real payout for some weeks without acting on the Rust result, and compare outputs. What I'd watch: latency per calculation, since this runs 25,000 times a night and needs to stay fast in aggregate, and a mismatch count against the Java result, broken down by currency pair, since I'd expect rounding differences to cluster there first. I don't have a real boundary-cutting example to point to yet since I haven't done this in production, so I want to be clear this is a plan built on the batch system I already know well, not a proven track record.
c015.java_ops: We had a slow memory leak on the payout-batch workers that took me three separate on-call weeks to actually nail down. Heap usage climbed steadily during each overnight batch run and triggered full GCs that stretched from 200ms to over 4 seconds by the end of a run, which pushed a handful of payouts past our processing window. I took heap dumps at the start, middle, and end of three separate batch runs and diffed them, which showed a growing collection of currency-conversion-rate objects that a caching layer was supposed to expire but wasn't, because the expiry check only ran on cache reads and nothing was reading stale entries once a currency pair went quiet for a few hours. I fixed it with an active eviction thread that sweeps the cache every 10 minutes regardless of read activity, instead of relying on lazy expiry. Full-GC pause length dropped back to under 300ms consistently, and we haven't seen a batch miss its window since, over roughly a year and a half of nightly runs.
c015.rust_readiness: No production Rust, I'll say that plainly. What I've done is spend evenings over the last several months building a small tool that recomputes multi-currency settlement totals from our payout export, partly to learn Rust and partly because I genuinely wanted a faster version of a script that used to take our finance team ten minutes to run in Excel. I'm maybe 80 hours in.
